deck.title: Periodicity of Physical Properties of the Elements in Period 3

front_blocks.md: Define **periodicity**.

back_blocks.md: **Periodicity** is the repeating pattern of chemical and physical properties shown by elements across the periods of the periodic table.

cards.back_md: **Periodicity** is the repeating pattern of chemical and physical properties shown by elements across the periods of the periodic table.

front_blocks.md: Why does atomic radius decrease across Period 3?

back_blocks.md: Atomic radius decreases across Period 3 because the **nuclear charge** increases with each additional proton, while the number of electron shells stays the same (so **shielding** is constant). The stronger attraction pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus.

cards.front_md: Why does atomic radius decrease across Period 3?
cards.back_md: Atomic radius decreases across Period 3 because the **nuclear charge** increases with each additional proton, while the number of electron shells stays the same (so **shielding** is constant). The stronger attraction pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Shielding increases across Period 3, causing atomic radius to decrease.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

Shielding remains roughly constant across Period 3 because all elements have the same number of electron shells. It is the increasing **nuclear charge** that pulls electrons closer, reducing the atomic radius.

front_blocks.md: Across Period 3, cations are **..........**  than their parent atoms because they have **..........**  electrons and reduced shielding.

back_blocks.md: Across Period 3, cations are **smaller** than their parent atoms because they have **fewer** electrons and reduced shielding.

cards.front_md: Across Period 3, cations are **..........**  than their parent atoms because they have **..........**  electrons and reduced shielding.
cards.back_md: Across Period 3, cations are **smaller** than their parent atoms because they have **fewer** electrons and reduced shielding.

front_blocks.md: Why are Period 3 anions larger than their parent atoms?

back_blocks.md: Anions gain one or more electrons into their outer shell, increasing **electron-electron repulsion**. The **nuclear charge** stays the same, so the electron cloud spreads out, making the ion larger than the parent atom.

cards.front_md: Why are Period 3 anions larger than their parent atoms?
cards.back_md: Anions gain one or more electrons into their outer shell, increasing **electron-electron repulsion**. The **nuclear charge** stays the same, so the electron cloud spreads out, making the ion larger than the parent atom.

front_blocks.md: Define **atomic radius**.

back_blocks.md: An **atomic radius** is the distance between the nucleus and the outermost electron of an atom, measured as half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element.

cards.back_md: An **atomic radius** is the distance between the nucleus and the outermost electron of an atom, measured as half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms of the same element.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Silicon has the highest melting point of all Period 3 elements.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
**Silicon** has a giant covalent structure with strong covalent bonds throughout, giving it the highest melting point in Period 3.

front_blocks.md: Electrical conductivity across Period 3 increases from Na to **..........**  and then **..........**  significantly for P, S, Cl and Ar.

back_blocks.md: Electrical conductivity across Period 3 increases from Na to **Al** and then **decreases** significantly for P, S, Cl and Ar.

cards.front_md: Electrical conductivity across Period 3 increases from Na to **..........**  and then **..........**  significantly for P, S, Cl and Ar.
cards.back_md: Electrical conductivity across Period 3 increases from Na to **Al** and then **decreases** significantly for P, S, Cl and Ar.

front_blocks.md: Explain the trend in ionic radius from Na<sup>+</sup> to Si<sup>4+</sup> across Period 3.

back_blocks.md: From Na<sup>+</sup> to Si<sup>4+</sup>, ionic radius **decreases** because the increasing **nuclear charge** attracts the electrons in the second principal quantum shell more strongly, pulling them closer to the nucleus.

cards.front_md: Explain the trend in ionic radius from Na<sup>+</sup> to Si<sup>4+</sup> across Period 3.
cards.back_md: From Na<sup>+</sup> to Si<sup>4+</sup>, ionic radius **decreases** because the increasing **nuclear charge** attracts the electrons in the second principal quantum shell more strongly, pulling them closer to the nucleus.

front_blocks.md: Why does the melting point increase from Na to Al across Period 3?

back_blocks.md: Na, Mg and Al have **giant metallic lattice** structures. Going from Na to Al, each atom donates more electrons to the delocalised 'sea' (1, 2 and 3 respectively), increasing the strength of **metallic bonding** and raising the melting point.

cards.front_md: Why does the melting point increase from Na to Al across Period 3?
cards.back_md: Na, Mg and Al have **giant metallic lattice** structures. Going from Na to Al, each atom donates more electrons to the delocalised 'sea' (1, 2 and 3 respectively), increasing the strength of **metallic bonding** and raising the melting point.

front_blocks.md: Define **metallic bonding**.

back_blocks.md: **Metallic bonding** is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a surrounding 'sea' of delocalised electrons.

cards.back_md: **Metallic bonding** is the electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a surrounding 'sea' of delocalised electrons.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Silicon is a good electrical conductor because it has a giant covalent structure.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Although **silicon** has a giant molecular (covalent) structure, it has no delocalised electrons, so it cannot conduct electricity easily. It is classified as a **semimetal** (metalloid).

front_blocks.md: P, S, Cl and Ar exist as **..........**  molecules with weak **..........**  forces between them, giving them low melting points.

back_blocks.md: P, S, Cl and Ar exist as **simple** molecules with weak **instantaneous dipole-induced dipole** forces between them, giving them low melting points.

cards.back_md: P, S, Cl and Ar exist as **simple** molecules with weak **instantaneous dipole-induced dipole** forces between them, giving them low melting points.

front_blocks.md: Why does sulphur (S<sub>8</sub>) have a higher melting point than phosphorus (P<sub>4</sub>)?

back_blocks.md: **Sulphur** exists as larger S<sub>8</sub> molecules compared to the smaller P<sub>4</sub> molecules. Larger molecules have stronger **instantaneous dipole-induced dipole** forces between them, so more energy is needed to separate them.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Aluminium is a better electrical conductor than sodium because it donates more electrons to the delocalised sea.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
**Aluminium** donates 3 electrons per atom to the delocalised sea compared to 1 from sodium, so there are more free electrons available to carry charge, making Al a better conductor.

front_blocks.md: In metals, the **..........**  electrons from the valence shell are free to move, allowing the metal to conduct **..........** .

back_blocks.md: In metals, the **delocalised** electrons from the valence shell are free to move, allowing the metal to conduct **electricity**.

cards.back_md: In metals, the **delocalised** electrons from the valence shell are free to move, allowing the metal to conduct **electricity**.

front_blocks.md: Why does silicon have the highest melting point in Period 3?

back_blocks.md: **Silicon** has a **giant molecular structure** in which each Si atom is covalently bonded to four neighbouring Si atoms. These strong covalent bonds require a large amount of energy to break, giving silicon the highest melting point in Period 3.

front_blocks.md: Define **semimetal**.

back_blocks.md: A **semimetal** (metalloid) is an element with properties intermediate between metals and non-metals, such as **silicon**, which has a giant covalent structure but only very limited electrical conductivity.

cards.back_md: A **semimetal** (metalloid) is an element with properties intermediate between metals and non-metals, such as **silicon**, which has a giant covalent structure but only very limited electrical conductivity.
